title: TypeScript basic types versus C# built-in types
hook: If you know C#'s `int`, `decimal`, `bool`, and `string`, TypeScript's type menu looks smaller — but the differences in null handling, number precision, and compile-time-only safety trip up mixed-stack teams daily.

blocks.text: C# offers a rich set of **built-in value types** (`int`, `long`, `double`, `decimal`, `bool`, `char`) plus **`string`** as a reference type. TypeScript collapses numerics into a single **`number`** (IEEE 754 double) and adds **`bigint`** for large integers. There is no `decimal` primitive. C# has one **`null`**; TypeScript/JavaScript has **`null`** and **`undefined`**. C# types exist at run time in the Common Language Runtime (CLR); TypeScript types are **erased** when compiled to JavaScript — only the JavaScript values remain.

entries.plainDefinition: TypeScript removes type annotations during compilation. No run-time type information remains.
The floating-point standard used by JavaScript number and C# double. Cannot represent all decimals exactly.
entries.example: `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` in both TS and C# double

entries.plainDefinition: C# compiler annotations for nullable strings and objects. Analogous to TypeScript strictNullChecks.
A struct wrapping a value type to represent absence. TypeScript uses `number | undefined` instead.

blocks.text: Mixed C#/TypeScript teams share APIs via JSON, gRPC, and OpenAPI. A C# backend serializes `decimal` fees and numeric enums; the TypeScript frontend receives `number` and must validate. A C# `string?` with null maps to JSON `null`, but TypeScript must decide whether that is `null`, `undefined`, or both. Understanding these mappings prevents silent data corruption and interview mistakes.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: "C# picks numeric types at compile time with run-time enforcement. TypeScript has one number (double), types erase at emit, and null/undefined are two separate absent values."

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: int, long, byte → number or bigint
items.body: Use `number` for values within `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Use `bigint` for larger IDs.

items.title: decimal → number (with caution) or string
items.body: JSON has no decimal type. Serialize as string or integer cents. Parse with a decimal library on the TS side.

items.title: double, float → number
items.body: Direct mapping. Same floating-point imprecision in both.

items.title: bool → boolean
items.body: Direct mapping. Neither language treats bool as int.

items.title: string → string
items.body: Direct mapping. C# string is a reference type; TS string is a primitive.

items.title: char → string
items.body: TypeScript has no char type. Use a single-character string.

items.title: enum → union or number
items.body: Numeric C# enums deserialize as numbers — validate range. String enums map to literal unions.

snippet.label: Deserializing C# decimal as number — risky
snippet.explanation: Line 3: C# `decimal` becomes JSON number, typed as TS `number` (double). Line 8: multiplication uses IEEE 754 — not exact like C# decimal. Fix: serialize decimal as string or integer cents from the C# side.

snippet.label: Mapping C# nullable types
snippet.explanation: Lines 5–7: C# `string?` null maps to TS `string | null`. C# `int?` null maps to `number | null`. Optional property `email?` handles JSON absence (undefined). Line 10: `??` handles both null and undefined.

snippet.label: C# numeric enum deserialized safely
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: C# numeric enum values. Lines 7–11: valid set for range checking. Lines 13–16: JSON can deliver any number — TypeScript types do not validate at run time. Always validate C# enum values at the boundary.

blocks.title: Pitfalls for mixed-stack teams
blocks.body: Assuming TypeScript types validate JSON at run time. Mapping C# decimal to number without a rounding strategy. Treating JSON null as undefined (or vice versa) inconsistently. Expecting TypeScript enum behavior to match C# enum serialization. Forgetting that TypeScript types vanish after compilation.

blocks.text: In production APIs between C# and TypeScript, define the wire contract explicitly (OpenAPI, protobuf). Serialize `decimal` as string or integer cents. Map C# `DateTime` to ISO 8601 strings (TypeScript `string`, parse with a date library). Use `unknown` + schema validation (Zod) on the TS side — the compiler cannot protect against malformed JSON. C# NRT and TS strictNullChecks are both compile-time overlays; both require boundary validation. For gRPC with protobuf, generated TS types are closer to C# types but still erase at run time.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming TypeScript has decimal or int types. Saying types survive compilation. Not validating JSON enum values. Ignoring the null vs undefined distinction when deserializing C# nullable types.

interviewTakeaways: C# has int, long, decimal, double; TypeScript has number (double) and bigint.
TypeScript types erase at compile time — JSON validation is mandatory.
C# null maps to TS null; C# missing optional maps to undefined.
60s: One number type in TS. No decimal. Types erase. Two absent values. Validate enums and decimals at API boundaries.
Follow-up: how would you safely transfer decimal currency between C# and TypeScript?
commonPitfalls: Mapping decimal to number without mentioning precision loss.
Believing TypeScript types enforce JSON shape at run time.
Strong answer: 'Serialize decimal as string/cents. Validate enums. Use unknown + Zod at boundaries. strictNullChecks mirrors NRT but both are compile-time only.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript JSON.parse returns plain objects with no type information. TypeScript annotations are a compile-time overlay on this untyped data.
C# built-in types map to CLR types with run-time presence. TypeScript types are erased — the mapping is conceptual, not automatic.
